q: A 200 g orphaned kitten needs tube feeding. What is the maximum safe single-feeding volume, given neonatal stomach capacity of about 40 to 50 mL/kg?
o: About 9 mL
About 18 mL
About 5 mL
e: Stomach capacity is about 40 to 50 mL/kg, so 0.2 kg x 45 mL/kg is roughly 9 mL. Exceeding this volume risks reflux and fatal aspiration.

q: A 10-day-old kitten is hypothermic (91°F / 32.8°C), hypoglycaemic and recumbent. What is the correct initial sequence?
o: Rewarm to near-normothermia first, then give warm dextrose-containing fluids and withhold oral intake until normothermic.
Give warm oral dextrose immediately to correct the hypoglycaemia while the kitten is rewarmed.
Give an IO dextrose bolus first and delay rewarming until the blood glucose has normalised.
e: A cold gut has ileus, so feeding ferments milk and causes endotoxaemia. Rewarm first, then give warm dextrose-containing fluids, and feed only once normothermic.

q: A litter of 4-week-old kittens is ready to be weaned. Which method is correct?
o: Offer a warm semisolid kitten-food slurry in a shallow pan, finishing formula by 5 to 6 weeks.
Switch abruptly to dry kibble at 4 weeks and stop bottle feeding on the same day, offering water only.
Continue bottle feeding until 8 weeks and then offer dry kibble alone with a bowl of fresh water.
e: Weaning starts at 3 to 4 weeks with a warm semisolid slurry in a shallow pan, and weaning from formula is complete by 5 to 6 weeks.

q: A 3-day-old orphaned kitten is being bottle fed in a foster home. What are the appropriate feeding interval and ambient temperature?
o: Every 6 hours, at 75 to 80°F (24 to 27°C)
Every 2 to 3 hours, at 85 to 95°F (29 to 35°C)
Every 4 to 5 hours, at 95 to 100°F (35 to 38°C)
e: Neonates are fed every 2 to 3 hours for the first few days, then every 4 to 5 hours until 3 weeks. First-week environmental temperature is about 85 to 95°F (29 to 35°C), dropping about 5°F (2.8°C) each week.

q: A litter of kittens shows fading kitten syndrome. Which is part of correct supportive care?
o: Rewarm first, then tube feed with SC fluids, treat littermates and rule out panleukopenia.
Feed immediately by tube, then rewarm the kittens slowly over the following 24 hours.
Give oral dexamethasone to the whole litter and reassess the kittens again in 48 hours.
e: Rewarm before feeding, then provide supportive care (tube feeding, SC fluids, warming), treat littermates and rule out feline panleukopenia.

q: An orphan kitten weighs 100 g at birth. Which daily weight gain should prompt concern?
o: A gain under 7 g per day
A gain under 15 g per day
A gain under 3 g per day
e: Neonatal kittens should gain 10 to 15 g/day. A gain under 7 g/day is inadequate and signals a need for supplemental feeding or a health problem.

q: Why are kittens under 6 to 8 weeks of age generally not housed in the shelter?
o: They are at high risk of infection, so foster care is strongly preferred.
They cannot be vaccinated until 12 weeks, so housing them is unlawful.
Adopters will not consider kittens under 8 weeks of age.
e: Kittens under 6 to 8 weeks are at high infection risk and are best placed in foster care rather than housed in the shelter.

q: Which method can detect pregnancy earliest in a queen?
o: Ultrasonography, from about day 10
Abdominal palpation, from about day 14 to 17
Serum relaxin, from about day 25
e: Ultrasound can detect feline pregnancy as early as about day 10, palpation from day 14 to 17, and serum relaxin is elevated by about day 25. Gestation is about 65 days.

q: A male cat has permanent canines but small testes. Approximately how old is he?
o: About 6 to 9 months
About 12 to 14 months
About 3 to 4 months
e: Permanent canines with small testes suggest about 6 to 9 months, whereas mature testes suggest 12 to 14 months.

q: Cats in a ward cleaned with a quaternary ammonium disinfectant at four times the correct dilution develop hypersalivation, anorexia and tongue ulcers. What is the most likely cause?
o: A calicivirus outbreak that happened to coincide with the change in cleaning
Caustic mucosal injury from grooming residual quaternary ammonium off the fur
Systemic quaternary ammonium toxicity from inhalation alone
e: Improperly diluted quaternary ammonium compounds are caustic. Cats groom the residue off and develop glossal ulceration and hypersalivation.

q: Why are cats uniquely sensitive to permethrin?
o: They lack hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes altogether, so the drug cannot be metabolised.
They have low plasma protein binding, so free drug reaches the brain quickly.
They have deficient hepatic glucuronidation (UGT), which impairs conjugation and prolongs exposure.
e: Cats have a UGT (glucuronidation) deficiency, not a complete absence, which contributes to permethrin sensitivity through accumulation of potent metabolites.

q: Which best explains feline acetaminophen toxicity, with methaemoglobinaemia and Heinz-body anaemia?
o: Direct renal tubular necrosis from accumulation of unmetabolised parent drug in the kidney
Deficient glucuronidation plus lack of N-acetyltransferase 2, with p-aminophenol driving methaemoglobinaemia
Hepatic glutathione depletion that causes centrilobular necrosis as the only mechanism of toxicity
e: Feline acetaminophen toxicity is multifactorial: deficient UGT glucuronidation plus NAT2 deficiency, with p-aminophenol producing methaemoglobinaemia.

q: Which pair of items is a recognised feline toxicant to avoid in a shelter?
o: Catnip and cat grass
Plain cooked chicken and canned tuna in water
Baby food containing onion powder, and lilies
e: Onion (including onion-powder baby foods) causes haemolytic anaemia, and lilies are nephrotoxic. Both must be avoided in cats.

q: An 11-year-old arthritic dog has been in the shelter for 5 months. It is reactive, anorexic and curled in the back corner 90% of the time. Which finding best indicates an unlivable quality-of-life state?
o: Refusal of a single meal on the day of a veterinary examination or a kennel move
Constant hypervigilance, no relaxed rest, and a persistent shift toward unpleasant states
Barking at unfamiliar people when the dog is confined at the front of the kennel
e: Quality of life is the balance of pleasant and unpleasant feelings. Persistent hypervigilance, no relaxed rest and dominance of unpleasant states indicate an unlivable state.

q: On the Villalobos HHHHHMM quality-of-life scale (seven variables, each scored 0 to 10), which total generally indicates that quality of life has become unacceptable?
o: Below 35 out of 70
Below 50 out of 70
Below 20 out of 70
e: Each of the seven variables is scored 0 to 10. A total above 35 suggests acceptable quality of life, and below 35 suggests it has become unacceptable.

q: What does an AAFCO statement of nutritional adequacy on a pet food label indicate?
o: That the diet has been tested and approved by the US FDA
The proportion of ingredients that come from human-grade sources
How the diet meets nutritional requirements, and for which life stage
e: The statement indicates nutritional adequacy and life stage. AAFCO sets pet food standards but does not approve individual diets.

q: Which nutrients must cats obtain pre-formed because they cannot synthesise them adequately?
o: Taurine, vitamin C and vitamin K
Taurine, arginine and vitamin A
Lysine, vitamin E and vitamin D
e: As obligate carnivores, cats require pre-formed taurine, arginine and vitamin A, which a meat-derived diet supplies. They can synthesise vitamin C.

q: What is the standard ceiling for treats as a fraction of an animal's daily caloric intake?
o: No more than 25%
No more than 20%
No more than 10%
e: The standard is the 10% rule: treats should not exceed 10% of daily calories.

q: Why are raw diets discouraged for shelter cats and dogs?
o: They supply too little protein for adult cats and cause vitamin C deficiency.
They are seldom nutritionally balanced and carry a risk of bacterial contamination and zoonotic infection.
They cause dental disease and are not digestible by dogs.
e: Raw and home-cooked diets are seldom balanced and carry contamination and zoonotic risk, including Salmonella. The ASV also raises regulatory concerns in multi-animal facilities.

q: What is the difference between resting energy requirement (RER) and maintenance energy requirement (MER)?
o: RER is energy for maintenance, whereas MER is the energy needed at complete rest.
RER applies to dogs only, whereas MER applies to cats only.
RER is baseline resting energy, whereas MER multiplies RER by a life-stage and activity factor.
e: RER is the resting energy requirement. MER multiplies RER by a life-stage and activity factor for maintenance.

q: Why are large, deep-chested dogs fed twice daily or more often?
o: To prevent obesity by limiting the size of each meal
To help reduce the risk of gastric dilatation-volvulus
To slow growth and reduce the risk of developmental orthopaedic disease
e: Splitting feeding across the day helps reduce the risk of gastric dilatation-volvulus in large, deep-chested dogs.

q: Which feeding method is most appropriate for a group-housed room of healthy cats?
o: A single large meal of canned food in a shared dish, removed after 4 hours
Canned food left out for free-choice feeding throughout the day
Free-choice dry food that is kept fresh and topped up, with monitoring, because non-eaters can be missed
e: Free-choice dry food suits group-housed cats because canned food spoils, but the cats must be monitored because those not eating can go unnoticed.

q: An obese cat (body condition score 8/9, 7 kg / 15.4 lb) has eaten nothing for 4 days in the shelter. What is the highest-priority concern?
o: Diabetic ketoacidosis from insulin resistance and stress
Acute kidney injury from dehydration and reduced water intake
Hepatic lipidosis from fat mobilisation into the liver during voluntary anorexia
e: Obese cats that mobilise peripheral fat during anorexia are at high risk of hepatic lipidosis. Veterinary examination and assisted feeding are indicated within 48 to 72 hours.

q: What is the principal danger when refeeding a chronically starved animal?
o: Acute pancreatitis from the fat content of a high-calorie first meal in a starved animal
Refeeding syndrome, with phosphate, potassium and magnesium shifts causing weakness and seizures
Hypercalcaemia from rapid mobilisation of bone calcium once food is reintroduced
e: Rapid refeeding causes dangerous electrolyte shifts (refeeding syndrome), so nutrition is reintroduced gradually with monitoring.

q: How often must uneaten food be discarded in shelter feeding protocols?
o: At least every 48 hours, unless it is visibly spoiled
At least every 24 hours, and immediately if contaminated or pest-infested
At least once a week, at the time of the full clean
e: Uneaten food is discarded at least every 24 hours, and immediately if it is contaminated or infested by pests.

q: A shelter cat on an exclusively dry diet develops recurrent urinary crystals. Which nutritional factor is most likely contributing?
o: Insufficient voluntary water intake, producing chronically concentrated urine
Excessive dietary taurine, producing alkaline urine
Excess dietary moisture, which dilutes the urinary buffer
e: Dry-only diets increase urine concentration. Cats have a low thirst drive relative to their needs (about 50 mL/kg/day, nearly double what a wet-food cat needs to drink).

q: Which findings indicate approximately 5% dehydration on physical examination?
o: Depression, a weak pulse and a prolonged capillary refill time
A skin tent persisting over 1 to 2 seconds, tacky or dry mucous membranes and sunken eyes
A normal physical examination with a mildly raised packed cell volume
e: At 5% or more: persistent skin tent, tacky or dry membranes and sunken eyes. At 10% or more: depression, weak pulse and prolonged capillary refill time.

q: Which water delivery method is preferred in a shelter with biosecurity concerns?
o: Individual water bowls for each animal or enclosure, cleaned daily
Community troughs that are refilled and scrubbed once a day
Shared bowls for each row of kennels, sanitised weekly
e: Community troughs are fomite risks. Individual bowls per enclosure, scrubbed on the same schedule as food bowls, are the biosecurity-correct approach.

q: What is the safe target rate of weight loss in an obese shelter cat?
o: About 3 to 5% of body weight per week
About 5 to 10% of body weight per week
About 1 to 2% of body weight per week
e: Safe loss is 1 to 2% of body weight per week with adequate protein and veterinary oversight. Faster loss mobilises fat more quickly than the liver can process and risks hepatic lipidosis.

q: For a 30 kg (66.1 lb) obese dog, what is the target weekly weight loss at the safe 1 to 2% rate?
o: About 30 to 60 g
About 1.5 to 3 kg
About 300 to 600 g
e: 1 to 2% of 30 kg is 300 to 600 g per week, which allows progress while avoiding the metabolic complications of crash dieting.

q: According to the 2026 ASV Guidelines for Humane Rabbit Housing, what is the rabbit comfort zone temperature range?
e: The rabbit comfort zone is 59 to 72°F (15 to 22°C). Rabbits are very sensitive to heat stress above 86°F (30°C).

q: A rabbit has been in a minimum-acceptable enclosure of 0.9 sq m (9.7 sq ft) for 3 weeks while awaiting surgery. What does this represent, and what is required?
o: Acceptable practice, provided that the rabbit receives daily time outside the enclosure for exercise.
Acceptable practice, because minimum-acceptable enclosures may be used for up to 4 weeks at a time.
A welfare compromise: this size is for stays under 2 weeks, so the rabbit must move to larger housing or foster.
e: Minimum-acceptable enclosures (8 to 11 sq ft / 0.8 to 1 sq m) are for stays under 2 weeks only. Longer housing causes musculoskeletal and gastrointestinal problems and elevated stress.

q: What is the minimum recommended primary enclosure size for a single rabbit on a long-term shelter stay, per ASV 2026?
o: 20 sq ft (1.9 sq m), with a length of 5 ft (1.5 m)
11 sq ft (1.0 sq m), with a length of 4 ft (1.2 m)
33 sq ft (3 sq m), with a length of 9 to 10 ft (3 m)
e: 33 sq ft (3 sq m) with an unobstructed run of 3 m is the minimum recommended for long-stay single rabbits, including integrated exercise space accessible at all times.

q: Why are motion-activated lighting systems contraindicated in rabbit housing areas?
o: The sudden switching produces ultrasonic noise that damages rabbit hearing.
Nocturnal rabbit activity triggers them, disrupting the dark phase of the light cycle.
They provide light that is too dim for rabbits to eat and drink.
e: Rabbit activity at night triggers motion-activated systems, disrupting the dark phase of the circadian cycle, which impairs stress adaptation and immune function.

q: A rabbit released from a minimum-acceptable enclosure after 3 weeks launches across the room in explosive bursts of running. What does this behaviour most likely represent?
o: Normal play (binkying), indicating good welfare in the enclosure
Seizure activity from Encephalitozoon cuniculi infection
Activity rebound from behavioural deprivation in an undersized enclosure
e: Activity rebound is a recognised welfare indicator of prior behavioural deprivation in an undersized enclosure.

q: Which flooring type is contraindicated for rabbit primary enclosures per the ASV 2026 guideline?
o: Solid flooring covered with hay or bedding
Solid flooring covered with a washable fleece mat
Slatted, grid or wire flooring
e: Wire and slatted floors cause pododermatitis (sore hocks). Solid flooring with appropriate bedding is required.

q: What are the four components of a complete rabbit primary enclosure per ASV 2026?
o: A hiding space, a litter box, a heat source, and a raised platform for observing the room
A resting space, a feeding area, an exercise space, and a companion rabbit to share the enclosure
Hiding and resting space, an elimination area, an eating and drinking area, and exercise space
e: The four required components are hiding/resting space, an elimination area, an eating/drinking area and exercise/play space.

q: What litter box configuration is recommended for shelter rabbits per ASV 2026?
o: At least one large box per rabbit, in a corner or periphery, with hay accessible from inside the box
One small corner-style box per rabbit, with hay offered in a rack elsewhere in the enclosure
One shared box for each pair of rabbits, placed in the centre of the enclosure
e: One large box per rabbit, at the periphery, with hay accessible from within is required. Corner-style boxes are too small even for small rabbits.

q: Why is acetic acid (vinegar) useful in rabbit housing sanitation?
o: It dissolves alkaline mineral deposits from rabbit urine that standard alkaline soaps cannot remove.
It inactivates rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus on caging and litter boxes.
It masks the odour of rabbit urine and so reduces stress in the rabbits.
e: Rabbit urine is alkaline and mineral rich, so alkaline soaps cannot dissolve the deposits. Acetic acid breaks down calcium and mineral build-up before or in place of standard disinfection.

q: What is the correct cleaning order when both healthy rabbits and RHDV-exposed animals are present?
o: Healthy kits, then healthy adults, then unhealthy rabbits, with RHDV-exposed animals last and using separate supplies
RHDV-exposed animals first, so that the highest-risk area is cleaned while the cleaner is fresh
Healthy adults, then RHDV-exposed animals, then healthy kits, with shared supplies
e: Clean from most vulnerable to most infectious. RHDV-exposed animals are cleaned last to prevent environmental contamination spreading to the healthy population.

q: What co-housing requirement applies to all group-housed rabbits per ASV 2026?
o: Only males must be neutered, because females rarely fight in groups.
All must be littermates, because unrelated rabbits cannot bond.
All must be spayed or neutered, because co-housing intact adults risks serious fighting.
e: All rabbits in group housing must be sterilised. Co-housing intact adults risks injury and death from fighting, and opposite-sex rabbits should be separated for a minimum of 2 weeks after sterilisation.

q: A shelter rabbit is scheduled for spay surgery next week. What is the ideal perioperative housing arrangement?
o: Housing next to the dog recovery area so that the rabbit can be monitored closely
Quiet housing separated from dogs, cats and ferrets, with bonded companions kept together
Housing alone in a dark room with no companions, even if the rabbit is bonded
e: Perioperative rabbit housing must be quiet and separated from predator species. Surgery is scheduled on days without cat or dog surgeries, and bonded pairs are kept together to reduce stress.

q: Which set of properties characterises rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus (RHDV) for shelter management?
o: An enveloped virus that is reportable and is readily inactivated by quaternary ammonium compounds
A non-enveloped calicivirus that is reportable and needs disinfectants active against non-enveloped viruses
A non-enveloped virus that is not reportable and affects mainly neonatal rabbits under 2 months
e: RHDV is a non-enveloped calicivirus and a reportable disease of rabbits over 2 months (neonates are resistant). Use accelerated hydrogen peroxide, potassium peroxymonosulfate or 0.5% sodium hypochlorite.

q: Why is oral penicillin contraindicated in rabbits, and how is rabbit syphilis treated?
o: Rabbits cannot absorb penicillin from the gut, so an intramuscular tetracycline is used.
It disrupts the caecal flora and causes fatal Clostridium overgrowth, so injectable penicillin G is used.
Penicillin is ineffective against Treponema in rabbits, so metronidazole is used.
e: Enteral penicillin disrupts caecal flora and causes fatal antibiotic-associated enterotoxaemia. Rabbit syphilis (Treponema paraluiscuniculi) is treated with injectable penicillin G.

q: Which flea product is contraindicated in rabbits?
o: Imidacloprid
Fipronil
Selamectin
e: Fipronil is associated with toxicity and death in rabbits. Imidacloprid and selamectin are generally safe, although selamectin is metabolised faster than in cats. Dog and cat tick products, collars and dips must also be avoided.

q: A dwarf-breed shelter rabbit develops head tilt, nystagmus and hind-limb paresis. Which is the most likely cause?
o: Pasteurella multocida otitis interna
Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis
Encephalitozoon cuniculi infection
e: In dwarf breeds, vestibular disease is most often Encephalitozoon cuniculi, an intracellular microsporidian. In standard breeds, Pasteurella otitis is more likely. Serology does not correlate with severity.

q: A ferret is vaccinated against canine distemper at shelter intake. Twenty minutes later it is lethargic, vomiting and collapsing. What is the most likely diagnosis and first-line treatment?
o: Vaccine anaphylaxis: diphenhydramine 2 to 4 mg/kg IM or IV and supportive care, epinephrine if severe
Vaccine-induced distemper: supportive care and isolation from other ferrets for at least 14 days
Hypoglycaemia from insulinoma: an IV dextrose bolus followed by small frequent meals every few hours
e: Ferrets have a high prevalence of anaphylactic reactions to distemper and rabies vaccines, typically within about 25 minutes. Diphenhydramine is first line, with epinephrine, dexamethasone and oxygen as needed.

q: Canine distemper virus is confirmed in a shelter ferret. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Supportive care and isolation for 14 days, because some ferrets recover fully with treatment
Treatment with an antiviral drug and keeping the ferret with its bonded companion for comfort
Humane euthanasia, as the disease is uniformly fatal, and vaccination of healthy unvaccinated contacts
e: Distemper is 100% fatal in ferrets with no effective treatment. Euthanasia minimises suffering and outbreak risk, and unvaccinated contacts are vaccinated.

q: A 2-year-old spayed female ferret develops bilateral symmetrical alopecia starting at the tail base and progressing towards the head, with vulvar swelling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Adrenocortical disease
Sarcoptic mange
Insulinoma
e: Bilateral symmetrical alopecia progressing from tail to head, with vulvar swelling in a spayed female, is the classic presentation of adrenocortical disease.

q: A guinea pig has severe pruritus, excoriations and seizure-like scratching episodes, and skin scraping confirms a mite infestation. What is the mite and its zoonotic status?
o: Chirodiscoides caviae, which is not zoonotic
Psoroptes cuniculi, which is zoonotic and causes ear canker in people
Trixacarus caviae, which is zoonotic and can cause temporary pruritic lesions in people
e: Trixacarus caviae, the sarcoptic mite of guinea pigs, causes severe pruritus that can mimic seizures and can temporarily infect people. Ivermectin 0.2 to 0.4 mg/kg SQ is repeated three times at 10 to 14 day intervals.

q: Why is vitamin C supplementation essential for guinea pigs in shelter care?
o: They cannot synthesise vitamin C and develop scurvy without dietary intake.
They excrete vitamin C rapidly through the kidney and need it only when ill.
They need it only during pregnancy and lactation.
e: Guinea pigs lack L-gulonolactone oxidase, so deficiency causes scurvy. Supplement with guinea pig pellets and fresh vegetables such as kale and bell peppers.

q: A shelter coordinator proposes pine shavings as bedding for guinea pigs. What is the correct response?
o: Shavings are acceptable because they are absorbent, generate little dust and control odour well.
Pine and cedar shavings are contraindicated (aromatic hydrocarbons); use paper-based or hardwood substrates.
Pine is acceptable for guinea pigs, but cedar should be avoided because it is too dusty.
e: Pine and cedar shavings contain aromatic hydrocarbons that cause respiratory irritation in guinea pigs and small rodents. Shredded paper, newspaper pellets and hardwood shavings are recommended.

q: Which shelter species can be asymptomatic carriers of Bordetella bronchiseptica that infect guinea pigs?
o: Birds, reptiles and amphibians
Only other guinea pigs
Rabbits, dogs, cats and non-human primates
e: Bordetella bronchiseptica has a broad host range. Rabbits, dogs, cats and non-human primates can be asymptomatic carriers, and even sharing the same airspace can be enough for transmission.

q: Which disinfectants are contraindicated in reptile and amphibian enclosures?
o: Phenolic compounds and glutaraldehyde
Dilute bleach (1:32) followed by thorough rinsing
Quaternary ammonium compounds followed by thorough rinsing
e: Phenolics and glutaraldehyde are toxic to reptiles and amphibians and must not be used. Dilute bleach and quaternary ammonium compounds are recommended, followed by thorough rinsing.

q: A rat has progressive respiratory noise, sneezing and chronic bronchopneumonia. Doxycycline plus enrofloxacin reduces the signs, but they return when antibiotics stop. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Sendai virus, a self-limiting infection that resolves in several weeks
Mycoplasma pulmonis, a lifelong infection that can be managed but not eradicated
Streptococcus pneumoniae, which is cured by a longer antibiotic course
e: Mycoplasma pulmonis is the most common major respiratory pathogen in rats. Infection is lifelong, and antibiotics control signs without eliminating it, so recrudescence on withdrawal is the norm.

q: What is 'wet tail' in hamsters, and which age group and mortality are typical?
o: Clostridium spiroforme enterotoxaemia in adult hamsters (over 6 months), with mortality under 10% treated
Lawsonia intracellularis ileitis in weanling hamsters (4 to 8 weeks), with mortality near 90% untreated
Salmonella septicaemia in geriatric hamsters (over 18 months), with mortality of about 30% treated
e: Wet tail is caused by Lawsonia intracellularis in stressed weanling hamsters. It needs aggressive fluids, antibiotics and nutritional support.

q: Which organism is the primary cause of rat-bite fever in humans?
o: Streptobacillus moniliformis
Pasteurella multocida
Bartonella henselae
e: Streptobacillus moniliformis is the primary cause. Wild and pet rats are asymptomatic carriers, and transmission is by bites, scratches, excreta or contaminated food and water.
